To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the HSV LTR promoter can drive long-term expression of beta-gal in the CNS, (2) the LTR promoter does not drive long-term expression in motor neurons, (3) expression of beta-gals in the hippocampal neurons drops considerably over time, but is still detectable at 2 months, and (4) expression of the LTR driven reporter gene in hippocampal cells is considerably less than expression of the same gene driven by the HSV tk promoter in
the LTR can drive long-term gene expression in CNS neurons, albeit at low levels.
(1) The LTR is active for long-term expression in hippocampal cells, but not in motor neurons.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a vector for the long-term expression of foreign genes.
the use of HSV as a vector for the expression of foreign genes.
the design of HSV vectors that are suitable for use in the CNS.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the LTR is a useful promoter for driving gene expression from the latent viral state for at least 2 months, and probably much longer.
HSV vectors containing the LTR promoter will be of use to study gene expression in the CNS.
the murine LTR can drive expression for long periods in neurons of the CNS.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HSV can be used as a vector for long-term expression of foreign genes, but only if the LTR is used as a promoter.
the LTR can be used to facilitate long-term reporter gene expression from HSV vectors in the CNS.
HSV vectors can be engineered to drive long-term gene expression in CNS neurons, although this expression is not as robust as that observed with other promoters in vitro.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the LTR is a useful promoter for driving long-term gene expression in the CNS.
the LTR can drive expression in CNS neurons, but that the levels of expression are low and that the LTR is less active in motor neurons.
the LTR can be used for long-term expression of foreign genes from the latent HSV genome in CNS neurons.
